abstract: Machine learning algorithms are increasingly used across scientific disciplines, but remain absent from several areas of comparative biology. One example is evolutionary model selection, which typically relies on likelihood-based methods to identify the model among a candidate set that best explains trait evolution across a phylogeny. This approach requires all candidate models to have a tractable likelihood function yet this may not the case for complex models. Alternative likelihood-free inference methods are available but their application is limited in scalability and flexibility. Both classes of methods struggle with discriminating models that yield statistically similar patterns in trait data. Here, I introduce a machine learning framework to perform evolutionary model classification from comparative data. Using simulated datasets, I demonstrate that the approach improves model discriminability relative to conventional likelihood-based model fitting but does not overcome model non-identifiability. I then revisit an analysis of early burst signals in comparative data to assess how a machine learning approach alters the patterns of early burst support obtained through likelihood-based inference. Finally, I discuss future extensions of this framework and their potential to improve both our representation and understanding of evolutionary process-to-pattern mapping.
